title: Cumulative Distribution and Tie Handling
description: Compute percentiles and deciles with NTILE and CUME_DIST while handling ties predictably.

data.text: Marketing wants customers split into value quartiles, and also wants the exact percentile of each customer's spend. The first attempt with `NTILE(4)` put customers with identical spend into different quartiles, which the business says is wrong. Write both the quartile assignment and the percentile, and explain the tie behaviour.

data.title: SQL Solution
data.code:
-- NTILE is an even split: it fills quartiles by row count,
-- so identical values CAN land in different quartiles.
SELECT
    CustomerId,
    TotalSpend,
    NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY TotalSpend DESC) AS SpendQuartile
FROM CustomerTotals;

-- CUME_DIST gives the fraction of rows with a value <= this row,
-- so ties all receive the SAME value.
SELECT
    CustomerId,
    TotalSpend,
    CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY TotalSpend)          AS CumeDist,
    PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY TotalSpend)       AS PercentRank,
    ROUND(CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY TotalSpend) * 100, 1) AS Percentile
FROM CustomerTotals;

-- Tie-safe quartiles derived from the distribution itself (1 = lowest spend)
WITH Dist AS
(
    SELECT
        CustomerId,
        TotalSpend,
        CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY TotalSpend) AS cd
    FROM CustomerTotals
)
SELECT
    CustomerId,
    TotalSpend,
    CASE WHEN cd <= 0.25 THEN 1
         WHEN cd <= 0.50 THEN 2
         WHEN cd <= 0.75 THEN 3
         ELSE                 4 END AS SpendQuartile
FROM Dist;

data.title: Explanation
data.text: `NTILE(n)` divides the ordered rows into `n` buckets of as-equal-as-possible **row count** — the buckets are equal in rows, not in value, and it will happily split identical values across two quartiles (the split depends only on position in the row number ordering). `CUME_DIST()` returns, for each row, the proportion of rows whose value is less than or equal to it, so **all peers share one value** — exactly what the business wants. `PERCENT_RANK()` is the other common function: it returns `(rank - 1) / (rows - 1)`, which means the minimum is always 0 and the maximum is always 1. Rule of thumb: use `NTILE` when you specifically need equal-sized groups (top 100 customers), and use `CUME_DIST`/`PERCENT_RANK` when you need a value-based distribution that respects ties (quartiles, deciles, percentiles).
